results.content:
# Novels in Translation: Les Misérables  
Les Misérables is perhaps best known as a stage musical and a film from 2012 starring Hugh Jackman, but the moving story was originally a novel written by Victor Hugo, which at 1,900 pages in its original French is approximately four times longer than the average Harry Potter book. First published in 1862, it is considered one of the greatest novels of the 19th century, although its gargantuan length is a possible explanation for the greater popularity of the musical, which, in contrast, is under three hours.
The length of these digressions is not surprising given that Hugo started Les Misérables with the intention of creating a controversy around the French judicial system, so a passionate social commentary seems appropriate – and he certainly had time for it, since it took him 20 years to complete the novel. But the text developed over this time to become more than a social commentary; it also evolved into a hopeful reflection on revolution and a means of applying philosophy to the degradation of France’s lower classes. So the lengthy deviations that seem irrelevant to the action could actually be seen as central to the novel’s purpose.  
Knowing this doesn’t make it any easier to plough through 1,900 pages. But it does make the length worthwhile, since Hugo’s extensive explanations show his passion for revealing the context of the characters’ suffering. These characters represent, as Hugo himself said, the masses and masses of people in 19th century France who had been denied ‘work and wages, food and warmth, courage and goodwill’, who desperately needed help because ‘it is rare for those who have sunk so low not to be degraded in the process, and there comes a point, moreover, where the unfortunate and the infamous are grouped together, merged into a single fateful word’. Misérables.
The novel has been translated into 21 languages, and there are 7 different translations into English which English-speaking readers can choose from. The first, by Charles E. Wilbour, came out during Victor Hugo’s lifetime and is considered the most faithful to the original novel and its context, though a more recent translation, such as Julie Rose’s 2007 version, may be an easier read for modern audiences. So there are plenty of options to access the breathtaking plot and the illuminating, apparently unrelated digressions – as long as you have four Harry Potters’ worth of enthusiasm, go for it!

results.name: Les Misérables songwriter felt a insufficient acknowledgment, collection of documents reveals
results.content:
# Les Misérables songwriter felt a insufficient acknowledgment, collection of documents reveals  
The deceased Herbert Kretzmer, who created the English libretto for Les Misérables, believed he was not properly acknowledged for transforming the original French musical into the widely acclaimed English-language version, correspondence have disclosed.  
They were uncovered in the archive of Kretzmer, who died in 2020 at 95 years old, after it was contributed to Cambridge University Library.  
A message that Kretzmer sent to theatre producer Cameron Mackintosh in 1987 referenced "negative measures taken by others to diminish my acknowledgment and contribution".  
> "I believe it will clarify matters if I explain, for the first and I trust only time, the clear and confirmable reality about the creation of the English adaptation of Les Miserables," he wrote.  
"Few individuals have had the opportunity to compare my English adaptation, page for page with the French source material.  
"Thus permit me, as concisely as I can, highlight the proof for asserting that, in terms of the real words now being sung regularly in both cities, there is very little indeed that can be considered translation.  
"The musical in English is essentially a original, reworked musical."  
He described it as "a mass of work that is so totally reconceived and rewritten that there is not any any substantial similarity between my lyrics and the original French version."
"I'm sorry that this message has to be created at all, but in light of the disagreeable steps taken by others to downgrade my recognition and contribution, I must stress that the musical is not a production translated or re-written, but a production revitalized," he commented.
## Word changes uncovered  
Dr Liz Savage, archive specialist at Cambridge University Library, assisted in organizing the Les Misérables parts of the archive.  
She discovered numerous modifications in Kretzmer's updated manuscript of the musical, including altering "ordinary" to "furious" in the number **Do You Hear The People Sing?**  
The number, which has been performed in demonstrations globally, starts: "*Do you hear the people sing?/ Singing the song of angry men.*"  
The archive also discloses how Kretzmer experimented with several alternative words initially, including "brave" and "bold", before deciding on "enraged".  
Documents also indicate that the number **Stars** was in jeopardy of being removed, before urging from Kretzmer and others to preserve it, writing: "We must entirely disassociate ourselves from the determination to eliminate Stars. We do not agree that the show is weakened by the inclusion of this song."  
Kretzmer's widow, Sybil, said: "The standing of Cambridge University shows the impact and influence of Herbert's work, and we are confident the collection will be maintained by the Library and continue for posterity, just like Les Miserables itself."

# Les Misérables lyricist expressed a insufficient acknowledgment, archive discloses  
The deceased Herbert Kretzmer, who penned the English lyrics for the famous musical, felt he was not given enough credit for adapting the original French musical into the widely acclaimed English-language version, letters have disclosed.  
They were found in the collection of Kretzmer, who passed away in 2020 aged 95, after it was given to the university's collection.  
A correspondence that Kretzmer sent to stage producer Cameron Mackintosh in 1987 discussed "negative measures taken by others to diminish my credit and input".  
> "I believe it will explain the situation if I spell out, for the first and I trust only time, the straight and verifiable reality about the creation of the English version of Les Miserables," he wrote.  
"Few individuals have had the chance to examine my English version, page for page with the French source material.  
"So let me, as succinctly as I can, highlight the indication for declaring that, in terms of the real words now being performed nightly in New York and London, there is hardly any indeed that can be called direct translation.  
"Les Miserables in English is virtually a fresh, rewritten production."  
He portrayed it as "a mass of material that is so completely reconceived and reworked that there is no longer significant resemblance between my words and the initial production."
"I regret that this letter has to be created at all, but in view of the unpleasant actions taken by others to downgrade my recognition and input, I must emphasize that Les Miserables is not a production translated or revised, but a production reborn," he stated.
## Text alterations discovered  
Dr Liz Savage, special collections assistant at the university, worked on documenting the Les Misérables portions of the collection.  
She discovered numerous edits in Kretzmer's revised version of the production, including changing "ordinary" to "angry" in the number **Do You Hear The People Sing?**  
The number, which has been sung in demonstrations internationally, commences: "*Do you hear the people sing?/ Singing the song of angry men.*"  
The archive also shows how Kretzmer experimented with multiple different terms originally, including "courageous" and "dauntless", before deciding on "enraged".  
Papers also reveal that the song **Stars** was in jeopardy of being eliminated, before pressure from Kretzmer and others to keep it, writing: "We need to completely disassociate ourselves from the decision to remove Stars. We disagree that the show is weakened by the inclusion of this number."  
Kretzmer's widow, Sybil, said: "The prestige of Cambridge University demonstrates the influence and impact of Herbert's work, and we are confident the archive will be conserved by the institution and live on for generations to come, just like Les Miserables itself."
